questions.problem:
Calculate the horizontal velocity of the eagle as a function of time.

The horizontal velocity of the bird is$\,$ 
{{field-1}}$\,\text{m/s}.$
questions.worked_solution:
The horizontal velocity of the eagle is given by ${x}^{′}(t),$ where 

$$
x(t)=\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{t}{5}).
$$

The formula for the derivative of arctangent is

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{arctan}⁡t)=\frac{1}{1+{t}^{2}}.
$$

Using the chain rule and the formula above, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{t}{5})) \\  & =\frac{1}{1+(t/5)^{2}}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{t}{5}) \\  & =\frac{1}{1+{t}^{2}/25}\cdot \frac{1}{5} \\  & =\frac{5}{25+{t}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the horizontal velocity of the eagle is given by the function ${x}^{′}(t)=\frac{5}{25+{t}^{2}}\,\text{m/s}.$

questions.problem:
The vertical velocity of the eagle increases at a rate proportional to the square of the time $t.$ In addition, the eagle loses $2\,\text{m/s}$ in the positive $y$-direction due to wind resistance. It is known that the eagle's vertical velocity equals $2\,\text{m}/\text{s}$ when $t=2\,\text{s}.$

The differential equation that describes the eagle's vertical velocity is ${y}^{′}(t)=$
{{field-1}}.
questions.worked_solution:
The vertical velocity increases proportionally with ${t}^{2}$ and decreases by $2.$ The differential equation that describes this is

$$
{y}^{′}(t)=k{t}^{2}-2,
$$

where $k$ is a (positive) constant of proportionality.

Since ${y}^{′}(2)=2,$ we can solve for $k:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(2) & =2 \\ k(2)^{2}-2 & =2 \\ 4k & =4 \\ k & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the differential equation is

$$
{y}^{′}(t)={t}^{2}-2.
$$

questions.problem:
The eagle's path traces a curve $C$ in the $xy$-plane. Suppose that the eagle is at the point $P$ on $C$ at time $t.$ Expressed in terms of $t,$ what function gives the slope of the tangent to $C$ at $P?$

The slope of the tangent to $C$ at time $t$ equals$\,$
{{field-1}}.
questions.worked_solution:
The slope of the tangent to $C$ equals $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}.$ To calculate this, we use the formula

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)}.
$$

In parts 1 and 2, we found

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=\frac{5}{25+{t}^{2}},\,{y}^{′}(t)={t}^{2}-2.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{t}^{2}-2}{(\frac{5}{25+{t}^{2}})}=\frac{1}{5}({t}^{2}-2)({t}^{2}+25).
$$

questions.problem: The tangent line to the eagle's flight path is horizontal at $t=${{field-1}}$\,\text{s}.$
questions.worked_solution:
The slope $m$ of a tangent line to a curve defined parametrically is given by

$$
m=\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)}.
$$

The tangent line is horizontal if ${y}^{′}(t)=0$ while ${x}^{′}(t)\ne 0.$

In parts 1 and 2, we found

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=\frac{5}{25+{t}^{2}},\,{y}^{′}(t)={t}^{2}-2.
$$

Solving ${y}^{′}(t)=0$ gives

$$
{t}^{2}-2=0\,⟹\,t=\pm \sqrt{2}.
$$

Note that $-\sqrt{2}\notin (0,\infty ),$ so we only consider the value $t=\sqrt{2}.$

Now, we note that

$$
{x}^{′}(\sqrt{2})=\frac{5}{27}\ne 0,
$$

which confirms that the curve's tangent is horizontal when $t=\sqrt{2}.$

questions.worked_solution:
If the eagle is descending, then its vertical velocity is negative.

We know that the eagle's vertical velocity is given by ${y}^{′}(t)={t}^{2}-2.$

To calculate the time interval in which the eagle's vertical velocity is decreasing, we solve the inequality ${y}^{′}(t)<0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(t) & <0 \\ {t}^{2}-2 & <0 \\ {t}^{2} & <2 \\ |t| & <\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

However, we know that $t>0.$ Therefore, the eagle is descending for $t\in (0,\sqrt{2}).$

questions.problem:
At time $t=5\,\text{s}$ the eagle is located at a point on $C$ with $y$-coordinate equal to $\frac{95}{3}\,\text{m}.$ Use the tangent line approximation to approximate the $y$-coordinate of the eagle's location when $t=\frac{110}{23}\,\text{s}.$

$y(\frac{110}{23})≈$
{{field-1}}$\,\text{m}$
questions.worked_solution:
The tangent line approximation to $y(t)$ at the point $a=5$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}L(t) & =y(a)+{y}^{′}(a)(t-a) \\  & =y(5)+{y}^{′}(5)(t-5).\end{aligned}
$$

We're told that $y(5)=\frac{95}{3},$ and since ${y}^{′}(t)={t}^{2}-2,$ then ${y}^{′}(5)=25-2=23.$ 

So, the tangent line approximation is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}L(t) & =\frac{95}{3}+23(t-5).\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can approximate $y(\frac{110}{23})$ by evaluating the tangent line approximation at $x=\frac{110}{23}.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}y(\frac{110}{23}) & ≈L(\frac{110}{23}) \\  & =\frac{95}{3}+23(\frac{110}{23}-5) \\  & =\frac{95}{3}+23(-\frac{5}{23}) \\  & =\frac{95}{3}-5 \\  & =\frac{80}{3}\,\text{m}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
The eagle's total displacement in the $y$-direction over the first $6$ seconds is given by ${\int }_{0}^{6}{y}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t.$ Calculate this displacement.

The eagle's total displacement in the $y$-direction over the first $6$ seconds is$\,$
{{field-1}}
$\,\text{m}.$
questions.worked_solution:
In part 7, we found that the antiderivative of ${y}^{′}(t)$ is

$$
y(t)=\frac{1}{3}{t}^{3}-2t+C.
$$

By the fundamental theorem of calculus, we take the antiderivative and evaluate the difference at the bounds:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{6}{y}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t & =y(t){|}_{0}^{6} \\  & ={(\frac{1}{3}{t}^{3}-2t)|}_{0}^{6} \\  & =(\frac{1}{3}(6)^{3}-2(6))-(\frac{1}{3}(0)^{3}-2(0)) \\  & =60-0 \\  & =60.\end{aligned}
$$

The eagle's total displacement in the $y$-direction over the first $6$ seconds is $60\,\text{m}.$

questions.problem:
Let $r(t)=⟨x(t),y(t)⟩$ be the position vector of the eagle. Find the distance between the eagle and its nest at time $t=5\,\text{s},$ rounded to two decimal places.

The eagle is approximately$\,$
{{field-1}}
$\text{m}$ away from its nest after $t=5$ seconds.
questions.worked_solution:
Since the nest is at the origin, the distance between the bird and its nest at time $t=5$ is $|r(5)|.$

We know that $y(5)=\frac{95}{3}.$ Evaluating the function at $t=5,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}r(5) & =⟨\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{5}{5}),\frac{95}{3}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{\pi }{4},\frac{95}{3}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the magnitude of this vector, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}|r(5)| & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\pi }{4})}^{2}+{(\frac{95}{3})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{16}+\frac{9\,025}{9}} \\  & ≈31.68\,\text{m}\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to two decimal places.

questions.worked_solution:
We differentiate each component separately.

* For the $x$-component, we have

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=\frac{5}{25+{t}^{2}},
$$

and therefore,

$$
{x}^{′}(\sqrt{5})=\frac{5}{25+(\sqrt{5})^{2}}=\frac{1}{6}.
$$

* For the $y$-component, we have

$$
{y}^{′}(t)={t}^{2}-2,
$$

and therefore,

$$
{y}^{′}(\sqrt{5})=(\sqrt{5})^{2}-2=3.
$$

So, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(\sqrt{5}) & =⟨{x}^{′}(\sqrt{5}),{y}^{′}(\sqrt{5})⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{1}{6},3⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

title: Finding the Motion of an Object Using Parametric Equations

shared_contexts.problem:
An eagle flies along the parametric curve

$$
x=\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{t}{5}),\,y=y(t),\,t>0,
$$

where $x$ and $y$ are measured in meters relative to its nest at the origin, and $t$ is measured in seconds. The functions ${x}^{′}(t)$ and ${y}^{′}(t)$ give the eagle's horizontal and vertical velocity, respectively.
